oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Social Capital at the Service of Informal Export: The Case of Moroccan Women Entrepreneurs
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: SALHI, Yasmine
MOUFDI, Nada
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This research explores the mobilization of informal social capital as a mechanism for circumventing institutional barriers to export among Moroccan women entrepreneurs. The study specifically examines how informal social networks compensate for the failures of the formal market and facilitate the internationalization of women-owned businesses in a constrained economic context. The empirical investigation relies on an exploratory qualitative approach following an abductive logic. The corpus of primary data was built from semi-structured interviews conducted with 14 Moroccan women entrepreneurs engaged in informal export activities. Thematic analysis, operationalized through NVivo 13 software, enabled the identification of recurring patterns and underlying mechanisms. The results reveal five main themes: (i) Export barriers; (ii) International marketing challenges; (iii) Informal export destinations; (iv) Informal export practices; (v) Informal social support networks. The entrepreneurs strategically mobilize their informal social capital to identify informal export opportunities and to develop alternative business practices that allow them to bypass institutional barriers. The qualitative nature of the study limits the statistical generalization of the findings. Comprehensive documentation of informal practices remains methodologically complex. The prescriptive implications suggest a reconfiguration of entrepreneurial support mechanisms, integrating the aspirations and recommendations directly voiced by the study participants. This bottom-up approach could facilitate the gradual formalization of export activities while preserving the flexibility necessary for these businesses. This research contributes to the academic literature by articulating four traditionally compartmentalized theoretical streams: international entrepreneurship, informal entrepreneurship, women’s entrepreneurship, and social capital theory, thereby shedding light on an underexplored phenomenon in the African context.
